To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the phage‐coded protein Gin is able to bind specifically to two sites in a specific configuration and that the binding is cooperative.
the invertase Gin binds to 34‐basepair sequences that flank the inverted G segment as inverted repeat.
The DNA invertase Gin binds specifically to inverted repeats flanking the G segment of phage Mu.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis for the site‐specific recognition of DNA sequences by the DNA‐binding protein Gin.
the molecular mechanisms of site‐specific recombination and the role of DNA bending in this process.
the molecular mechanism of site‐specific DNA inversion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IR is the binding site of Gin, and the inverted repeat configuration is the recognition sequence of the inversion reaction.
the IR is a binding site for Gin which contains at least two binding sites for the enzyme.
the Gin protein binds to the IR as a dimer in a sequence specific fashion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have identified a minimal site for Gin‐mediated inversion, and that we have shown that this site is not a single‐site binding site, but rather a site consisting of two binding sites for the same protein, one of which is bound only in the presence of the other.
the DNA inversion reaction is a two‐step process, in which Gin binds to the G segment first and then to the I segment, resulting in DNA bending.
the Gin binding site contains a 25 bp inverted repeat that is sufficient for inversion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Gin‐FIS system provides a paradigm for the study of site‐specific recombination.
the DNA invertase binds specifically to the DNA invertase binding sites and that the DNA invertases can bend DNA upon binding.
the DNA invertase of Mu binds specifically to the DNA inversion sites and bends DNA upon binding.
